thread.title: S&P 500 Gains 0.9% to Break Its Record—at Last

author: Ben Levisohn
title: S&P 500 Gains 0.9% to Break Its Record—at Last
text:
Photo: J. A. Hampton/Getty Images By Ben Levisohn Aug. 24, 2018 7:20 p.m. ET Finally. After nearly seven months since its Jan. 26 top, the S&P 500 once again hit a new all-time high.
The broad-market index gained 0.9%, to 2874.69, this past week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 121.03 points, or 0.5%, to 25,790.35. The Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.7%, to 7945.98, also an all-time high.
It sure took the S&P 500 long enough. The Nasdaq Composite broke its Jan. 26 high in March, and has racked up a total of 26 new records this year. The small-cap Russell 2000 cleared its Jan. 23 peak in May and also closed at an all-time high last week. And the Wilshire 5000, the broadest U.S. stock index, traded at a new record on Aug. 8.
Why was the S&P 500 late to the party? Part of the problem was that when one part of the market went up, another went down. When the FAANGs— Facebook (ticker: FB), Amazon.com (AMZN), Apple (AAPL), Netflix (NFLX), and Alphabet (GOOGL)—were flying high, not much else was working. Then Facebook and Netflix hit a little earnings-related turbulence, while sectors like consumer staples, health care, and utilities finally started to catch fire. This past week, though, nearly everything came together: Discretionary and tech bounced back, health care continued to shine, and materials and energy rallied.
More on the Markets
No, This Is Not the Longest Bull Market Ever Why Health Care’s Rally May Be Just Getting Started Rob Ginsberg, a technical analyst at Wolfe Research, calls the S&P 500’s late arrival to the party a good thing, especially since it came after a tough stretch by the FAANGs. “When you see that very crowded trade start to unwind, and the market holds up, that’s a pretty good sign,” he explains. “It’s been so resilient.”
Has it ever. Just consider everything the market has to absorb—or, as some would argue, ignore—to get there this past week. New tariffs went into effect as trade talks between China and the U.S. apparently went nowhere. The possible impeachment of President Donald Trump was in the headlines after Michael Cohen pleaded guilty to eight federal crimes . And the U.S. Federal Reserve appears set on a course to raise interest rates every three months.
But not everyone is happy with what they see. Doug Ramsey, chief investment officer at the Leuthold Group, points to the number of stocks making new lows in recent weeks as one worrisome trend, with 10% of Nasdaq stocks making 52-week lows on Aug. 17. He also notes the eye-popping number of new highs and new lows—another potentially bearish sign.
But not enough to get too bearish, Ramsey says, as long as other measures of breadth, like the so-called Advance-Decline Line, remain solid. Instead, he prefers to characterize the market as “fractured.”
Newsletter Sign-up The real sign that the bull market is nearing its end would be if tech and discretionary start to underperform—and don’t bounce back. Those two sectors have led the market higher, much as they did before the popping of the dot-com bubble, or financials did before the 2007 top.
“If there’s a wholesale shift in leadership from tech and discretionary to defensives, that would be a confirmation of the end of the cycle,” Ramsey says.
We may not be there yet, but remember—every new high has the potential to be the last one.
